title: Claude Code for Empirical Research: A Hands-On Session
text:
John Barrios · Yale School of Management · Prepared for Stanford PhD students


This session is for PhD students who do empirical research, in any field. Most of my examples use accounting and finance data, but the same steps work for any project that starts from raw data. You do not need any experience with Claude Code. Stata and Python users are both welcome.
Claude Code is an AI agent that runs in your terminal. Unlike a chat window, it can read your files, write and run code, look at the output, and fix its own errors. That saves a lot of time on work like cleaning data, merging files and rebuilding tables. It can also make mistakes quickly, and they can be hard to spot. So we spend as much time checking the agent’s work as using it.
Bring your laptop. Most of the three hours is hands-on.

Tuesday, November 3, 2026 · 12:00–3:00 pm · Room E247
3 hours · 2 labs · free SEC data only · about 2 hours of prep


Start with Before Class See the agenda →

title: Claude Code for Empirical Research: A Hands-On Session
Lab 2: A Skill and Three Verification Drills
text:
Download the starter pack (zip)  Slides  Agenda
Lab 2 has two parts. In Part A (about 25 minutes, after a short demo) you turn the pipeline you built in Lab 1 into a skill: a written procedure Claude loads by itself when a request matches it, so you never have to explain the pipeline again. In Part B (25 minutes) you run three short drills that check whether your project is safe to share and whether your results hold up for a reader who did not see you build them.
You need two files from the starter pack: SKILL_skeleton.md for Part A and lab2_verification_drills.md for Part B.

title: Lab 2: A Skill and Three Verification Drills
text:
Demo 2: EDGAR text to data
Before Part A, I show a five-minute demo that applies the same steps to text. Claude pulls the Risk Factors section (Item 1A) from a set of 10-Ks on EDGAR and counts a keyword in each one. Two details are worth copying in your own work. Every downloaded filing is cached, so a rerun fetches nothing it already has. And the pipeline writes a quality report that says how many sections it extracted and gives a reason for every one it missed. A count of successes without reasons for the failures doesn’t tell you whether to trust the measure.

title: Lab 2: A Skill and Three Verification Drills
section: Part A: turn your pipeline into a skill
text:
Part A: turn your pipeline into a skill
A skill is a folder holding a SKILL.md file. The file starts with a short header (the frontmatter) with a name and a description, followed by the steps of the procedure. Claude reads the description of every installed skill at the start of a session and loads the full steps only when a request matches it. So the description decides whether the skill ever runs.
Most first skills fail in the same way: the description reads as a title. Compare:
---
name: fsds-panel
description: FSDS data tool
---
---
name: fsds-panel
description: Use when the user asks to build a firm-year panel or a financial
  ratio from SEC Financial Statement Data Sets (FSDS), mentions sub.txt or
  num.txt, or asks for a median of an XBRL tag by year or industry.
---
The first says what the skill is. The second describes what a real request looks like, so Claude has something to match.
Build it.

In your Lab 1 folder, make the skill folder at project scope, so it travels with this project:
cd ~/stanford_lab && mkdir -p .claude/skills/fsds-panel
Copy SKILL_skeleton.md from the starter pack to .claude/skills/fsds-panel/SKILL.md.
In your Lab 1 session (or a new one in the same folder), ask Claude to fill in the skeleton from what you actually did: the inputs (which quarters, which tags, which aggregation), the steps in order, the filters, the paper-trail files, and the checks. Ask it to keep the steps general enough to work for a different tag.
Read the result. Rewrite the description yourself if it reads like a title. List the phrases a real request would use.
Make sure --- is on line 1 of the file, with no comment or blank line above it. Claude reads the frontmatter only when the file starts with it. Delete any leftover comments from the skeleton.

Test it. Don’t test in the session where you wrote the skill. That session already knows the pipeline, so it will do the work whether or not the skill fires.

Leave Claude (type /exit) and start a fresh session in the same folder with claude.
Ask for something the skill should handle without naming it, for a measure you did not build in Lab 1. For example: “What was the median ratio of long-term debt to total assets by fiscal year in the FSDS quarters in fsds/?”
Watch the transcript. If the skill fires, Claude says it is using the fsds-panel skill. If instead it starts reading your Lab 1 scripts or asking how the files are laid out, the skill did not fire. Rewrite the description and test again in another fresh session.
Confirm that the run follows your steps: the consolidated filter, DATA_PROFILE.md before any figure, and the paper trail.

You can always run a skill on purpose by typing /fsds-panel. That doesn’t test the description, so do the test above first.






TipVerify this: the skill




SKILL.md is at .claude/skills/fsds-panel/SKILL.md, with --- on line 1
The description lists phrases a real request would use, not a title
In a fresh session, a request that doesn’t name the skill makes it fire
The run follows the skill’s steps, including the consolidated filter and DATA_PROFILE.md

title: Lab 2: A Skill and Three Verification Drills
text:
Part B: three verification drills
Run all three on your own project. If you have a research repository on your laptop, use it for Drill 1, because that is where an exposed key would actually hurt you. Otherwise use ~/stanford_lab. Drill 1 needs a git repository. If your Lab 1 folder isn’t one yet, run git init and echo "fsds/" > .gitignore there, then ask Claude to commit your scripts.

Drill 1: the two-check credential audit
These two checks come from the full course’s Module 5, adapted for public data and API keys. Run both from the root of the repository. Both should come back empty. Paste both outputs into VERIFY_NOTES.md in the repo.
Check 1: has a credential file ever been committed?
git log --all --full-history --oneline -- '*.env' '*.env.*' '.mcp.json'
Expected output: nothing.
This looks for a .env file, or a variant such as .env.local, in any folder and at any point in the history, plus a project-level .mcp.json, which holds credentials if you ever registered an MCP server with project scope. If it returns even one commit, a credential file was committed at some point. Deleting the file now does not remove it from history. Anyone who clones the repo, including a coauthor, a referee running a replication package or a stranger on GitHub, can still find it in an old commit with git show <commit>:<path>.
Check 2: does your actual key appear anywhere?
In the full course this check searches for your WRDS password. This session uses no WRDS, so run it for each secret this project actually uses, such as an Anthropic or OpenAI API key or a GitHub token. Type read -s SECRET, paste the key (it won’t echo), and run the two searches with $SECRET:
read -s SECRET
git log --all --oneline -S"$SECRET"
git grep -l -F --untracked -e "$SECRET"
Expected output: nothing.

git log -S lists every commit that ever added or removed the key, including in a script you have since deleted.
git grep lists files git would pick up that contain it now. It skips gitignored files.

Both searches print commit IDs or file names, never the key. They look for the key itself, not the name of the variable that holds it, so a script that reads the key from the environment (the right way) passes, and a script with the key typed into it fails. Do not use a plain grep -r "API_KEY" . instead: it flags correct code and misses a key that was committed and later deleted.
If the project uses no secrets at all, run Check 1 and write “no secrets in this project” in VERIFY_NOTES.md for Check 2.






WarningIf either check finds something




Treat the credential as compromised right away. Do not assume it is fine because no one saw it. Assume any credential that has ever been committed to a git repository is exposed, even in a private repo and even if you never pushed it anywhere.
Revoke and rotate first, clean up second. Regenerate the API key (or change the password) before you touch the repository. If you clean the repo first and rotate later, the exposed credential stays valid while you work.
Remove it from history, not just the current version. Deleting the current copy is not enough while the secret is still reachable in git log history. A history rewrite with git filter-repo or BFG removes it. If the project is small and early, starting a fresh repository is simpler.
Confirm the fix by re-running both checks and getting a clean result before you consider the audit passed.





Drill 2: a clean-room referee
A session that watched you build the pipeline has heard all your reasons and tends to accept them. A referee has heard none of them. So give the review its own room: a fresh session in an empty folder that holds only what a reader of your paper would see, plus a deny rule that stops the session from editing it.

In ~/stanford_lab, write summary.md yourself, in about five minutes and without the agent. Include the figure caption, a short paragraph on how the sample was built (files, filters, tags and your tag choice), and the attrition table. Leave out DECISIONS.md and your scripts. A referee gets the paper, not your notes.
Build the room and start a fresh session in it. Replace my_figure.png with the name of your figure:
mkdir -p ~/referee_room/paper ~/referee_room/.claude
cp ~/stanford_lab/summary.md ~/referee_room/paper/
cp ~/stanford_lab/my_figure.png ~/referee_room/paper/
echo '{"permissions":{"deny":["Edit(./paper/**)"]}}' > ~/referee_room/.claude/settings.json
cd ~/referee_room && claude
Send this prompt:
You are refereeing a short empirical exhibit for an accounting journal. You
have only what is in paper/. Do not edit any file. Read the caption, the
sample description and the attrition table, and look at the figure. Write
the three most serious objections to review/referee.md, most serious first.
For each, say what claim it undermines and what evidence would answer it.
Check whether the stated filters can produce the N in the attrition table.
Aim the criticism at the exhibit, not the author.
Read review/referee.md. In VERIFY_NOTES.md, write down one objection you had stopped seeing. Then answer one objection in writing at the bottom of review/referee.md, not in the chat. In the chat, the model tends to give in.

Your personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, if you have one, still loads in this room, so keep project details out of it. If the report is mostly praise, ask again for the three most serious problems.


Drill 3: one deny rule, tested
A line in CLAUDE.md saying “never change the raw data” is a request. Claude usually follows it, but nothing enforces it. A deny rule in .claude/settings.json is enforced: Claude Code refuses the matching action in every permission mode.

In ~/stanford_lab, create .claude/settings.json (or add to it if it exists):
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Edit(./fsds/**)",
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)"
    ]
  }
}
Record a fingerprint of one raw file: shasum fsds/2024q1/readme.htm
Start a fresh session in the folder so the rules load (/exit, then claude). Run /permissions and check that the three rules are listed.
Ask: “Append the line ‘test’ to fsds/2024q1/readme.htm with your file edit tool. Then try a shell command, echo test >> fsds/2024q1/readme.htm. Quote any error you get.” Both attempts should be refused.
Run shasum fsds/2024q1/readme.htm again. It must match step 2. Paste the refusal text and both fingerprints into VERIFY_NOTES.md.
Commit .claude/settings.json, so anyone who works in the repo gets the same rules.

Know the limit. The rule blocks Claude’s file tools and shell commands that name the path. It does not stop a Python script that opens the file itself. Only an operating-system sandbox (/sandbox, or a container) blocks that.






TipVerify this: the drills




Check 1 run and its output pasted into VERIFY_NOTES.md
Check 2 run for each secret the project uses (or “no secrets” written down), with output pasted
review/referee.md exists in ~/referee_room, written by a session that saw only paper/
One objection you had stopped seeing in VERIFY_NOTES.md, and one answered in writing in the report file
Deny rules in .claude/settings.json, tested in a fresh session, with the refusal and both fingerprints in VERIFY_NOTES.md

title: After Class
text:
What to keep doing
Whatever tool you use next, keep doing these:

Ask for DATA_PROFILE.md, DECISIONS.md and LOG.md in the first prompt, before any analysis runs.
Check at least one number against a source the agent did not touch.
Test a skill in a fresh session before you trust it.

title: Readings
text: Read the two required papers before class, about 40 minutes in total. The discussion in the last twenty minutes of the session draws on them and on what you did in the labs. Each paper has two discussion questions below. Come with a short answer to at least one question per paper.

title: Readings
text:
Required

Brodeur et al. (2026): AI and reproducibility
Brodeur, Abel, et al. (2026). “AI-Assisted Teams Outperform AI-Led Teams but Not Human-Only Teams in Assessing Research Reproducibility in Quantitative Social Science.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 123(22): e2524747123. doi:10.1073/pnas.2524747123.
 Read the PDF (published version, 11 pages, 1 MB; open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, reposted unchanged)
What to read: the introduction and the results.
What it finds. The authors randomly assigned 288 researchers to 103 teams, which tried to reproduce published social-science results. Some teams worked without AI, some worked with AI assistance, and in some the AI led the work with little human oversight. Human-only teams reproduced 94 percent of results and AI-assisted teams 91 percent, but the human-only teams found significantly more of the major coding errors. AI assistance gave no measurable advantage over working without it. Teams where the AI led reproduced 37 percent.
Discussion questions.

In Drill 2 a fresh Claude session reviewed your work. In this study, teams with AI help caught fewer of the major errors than teams without it. What would an AI review need to look like for it to add to your own checking, and how would you know whether it did?
AI-led teams reproduced 37 percent of results. Think back to Lab 1: at which steps would the result have gone wrong if you had not been reading along, and which steps could you have left to the agent with little oversight?



Kusumegi et al. (2025): AI and scientific output
Kusumegi, Keigo, Xinyu Yang, Paul Ginsparg, Mathijs de Vaan, Toby E. Stuart, and Yian Yin (2025). “Scientific Production in the Era of Large Language Models.” Science 390(6779): 1240–1243. doi:10.1126/science.adw3000. Free author version at arXiv 2601.13187.
 Read the PDF (free arXiv version; the Science version is behind a paywall, so we link to arXiv rather than repost it)
What to read: the whole paper. It is four pages.
What it finds. The authors track 2.1 million preprints. Authors who adopt LLMs post between 24 and 89 percent more papers, depending on field and background. The usual link between complex writing and paper quality reverses, so polished prose stops being a sign of a good paper. Adopters also read and cite more widely, including younger and less-cited work.
Discussion questions.

If polished writing no longer tells a referee much about a paper’s quality, what will editors and referees look at instead? What does that mean for how you document and present your own work?
Suppose every PhD student in your field could do what you did today. If output per researcher rises by the amounts this paper reports, what happens to the review queue at the top journals, and to what a publication signals on the job market?

title: Readings
text:
Optional

Hao, Xu, Li and Evans (2026): AI methods and the focus of science
Hao, Qianyue, Fengli Xu, Yong Li, and James A. Evans (2026). “Artificial Intelligence Tools Expand Scientists’ Impact but Contract Science’s Focus.” Nature 649: 1237–1243. doi:10.1038/s41586-025-09922-y. Free author version at arXiv 2412.07727.
What to read: the whole paper, if you have time.
What it finds. This paper is about a different kind of AI use from the other two. It studies research that applies AI methods, mostly machine learning and deep learning, across about 41 million natural-science papers since 1980. Scientists whose work uses AI methods publish about three times as many papers, receive almost five times as many citations, and become project leaders earlier. Over the same period, the range of topics studied narrows by about 5 percent and scientists engage with each other’s work about a fifth less. The study is observational, and the authors say so: scientists who adopt AI methods differ from those who don’t in other ways too, so the comparison does not show that AI causes these gains.
Discussion questions.

The gains go to individual researchers, while the narrowing of topics affects the whole field. Do tools like the one you used today push you toward questions that public data answers easily? What would push back?
Because the study is observational, what alternative explanations would you want ruled out before believing that using AI methods causes higher output and citations? What data or design could rule them out?

title: Readings
text:
The three questions in class
The discussion at the end of the session takes one question from each of three areas. You don’t need to prepare for these separately; the paper questions above feed into them.

Learning. You produced results faster than usual today. Do you understand them as well as you would if you had built them by hand?
Verification. Two identical results, one hand-coded by a research assistant and one produced by an agent with a full paper trail. Should a referee treat them the same?
The market for papers. If producing a paper gets cheaper, which parts of your research stay hard to do? Those parts become more valuable.

title: Readings
text:
Going further
The full course’s Module 6 seminar uses three more readings on the same questions: a field experiment on learning with and without AI, a study of expert deskilling, and a system that writes machine-learning papers end to end. It also lists accounting-specific options. They are listed on its Module 6 page (access code Barrios_AI2026).

title: About John Barrios
text:
John Barrios is an Associate Professor of Accounting at the Yale School of Management and a Faculty Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, in the Political Economy and the Productivity, Innovation, and Entrepreneurship groups.
His research looks at how accounting information and the rules that govern it shape firms and the people who run them. He studies who enters the accounting profession, who starts a business, how politics affects the way people read and act on the numbers, and how disclosure regulation interacts with antitrust enforcement. His work has been published in the Journal of Accounting Research, the Journal of Public Economics, American Economic Journal: Microeconomics, Management Science and the Journal of Financial Economics.
He is Editor of Accounting Horizons, an Ad Hoc Advising Editor at the Journal of Accounting and Economics, and Guest Editor of the Journal of Labor Economics Symposium on Occupational Licensing. He co-founded the Labor and Accounting Group.
He also works on how researchers can use AI agents without giving up verification or ownership of their results. He teaches a PhD course on Claude Code for accounting research, of which this session is a short version, and maintains an open-source set of agent skills for empirical research, including a WRDS connector.
Before Yale, he taught at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and at the Olin Business School at Washington University in St. Louis. He holds a PhD in Business Administration and an MPA in Accounting from the University of Miami, and a BS in Industrial and Labor Relations from Cornell University.

title: Lab 1: From FSDS to a Verified Figure
text:
Download the starter pack (zip)  Slides  Agenda
In this lab you run the loop from the first demo yourself: raw SEC data in, a figure out, and a written record of every decision in between. You have 50 minutes. The data is already on your laptop from the Before Class page, so nothing in this lab depends on the room’s wifi except Claude itself.
You need three files from ~/stanford_starter:

title: Lab 1: From FSDS to a Verified Figure
text:
The data
You have three quarters of the SEC’s Financial Statement Data Sets in ~/stanford_lab/fsds/: 2016q1/, 2020q1/ and 2024q1/. FSDS groups filings by the quarter the SEC received them. Most US firms have a December year end and file their 10-K in February or March, so these three files hold mostly fiscal years 2015, 2019 and 2023. Group your results by the fiscal year column fy in sub.txt, not by the name of the folder.
Two files in each folder matter:

sub.txt has one row per filing: the accession number (adsh), the firm’s CIK, its SIC industry code, the form type, the fiscal year and the period the filing covers.
num.txt has one row per reported value: the accession number again, the XBRL tag (such as Assets), the date the value applies to (ddate), the number of quarters it spans (qtrs), the unit (uom), two fields called segments and coreg, and the value.

You join the two on adsh. Then four filters apply to every tier, and the opening prompt states all of them:

Consolidated rows only. Keep rows where segments and coreg are blank and uom is USD. A blank segments field means the value is for the whole firm rather than one business segment, and a blank coreg means it is for the parent filer rather than a co-registrant. About half the rows in a recent num.txt are segment values, so skipping this filter can count the same firm’s number several times.
10-Ks only. Keep form = 10-K.
The right qtrs. Use qtrs = 0 for balance-sheet values (stocks, such as Assets or cash) and qtrs = 4 for full-year flows (such as R&D expense).
One quarter at a time. Each num.txt is about 400 to 470 MB. Read one quarter, keep only the tags and columns you need, then move to the next, rather than loading all three at once.

A 10-K also reports last year’s numbers next to this year’s, so the same firm-year value can show up in two filings. Keep values whose ddate matches the filing’s own period end, and write that rule into DECISIONS.md.

title: Lab 1: From FSDS to a Verified Figure
text:
Choose your tier
Pick one. The tiers differ in how much cleaning judgment they ask of you. Pick the one that fits the time and your interests, not necessarily the hardest.
Base: cash holdings. Cash and cash equivalents divided by total assets, as the median across firms for each fiscal year. The numerator tag is CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue and the denominator is Assets, both with qtrs = 0. Check the cash tag’s coverage in DATA_PROFILE.md before you compute anything.
What to expect, from the class files (share of 10-Ks with a consolidated value for the filing’s own period end):









Tag
2016q1
2020q1
2024q1




Assets
98.4%
98.7%
99.4%


CashAndCashEquivalentsAtCarryingValue
91.3%
85.1%
80.5%


CashCashEquivalentsRestrictedCashAndRestrictedCashEquivalents
0%
57.5%
79.3%



The main cash tag loses coverage after the 2018 restricted-cash standard, as filers move to the tag that includes restricted cash. The median cash-to-assets ratio is about 7 to 9 percent, and part of the rise in the last year comes from which firms drop out of the main tag. Report the median both ways: main tag only, and with the restricted-cash tag as a fallback. Financial firms are more than a quarter of filers, so also say whether you keep them.
Standard: R&D intensity by industry. R&D expense divided by total assets: ResearchAndDevelopmentExpense with qtrs = 4 over Assets with qtrs = 0. Report the median by two-digit SIC code (sic2, the first two digits of sic in sub.txt) for the five largest sic2 groups, by fiscal year. You decide what “largest” means (most firms reporting R&D is the simplest choice) and record it in DECISIONS.md.
What to expect: ResearchAndDevelopmentExpense appears in 26 to 33 percent of 10-Ks in these files. By that count the five largest groups are SIC 28 (chemicals and pharmaceuticals), 73 (business services, including software), 38 (instruments), 36 (electronics) and 35 (machinery and computers). SIC 28’s median is far above the rest, above 20 percent of assets, because it holds hundreds of small biotechs.
Check at least one large firm against its 10-K. A tag name can mislead: in Johnson & Johnson’s fiscal 2023 filing, ResearchAndDevelopmentExpense is $483 million, a charge for buying in-process R&D, while its income-statement R&D of about $15.1 billion sits under ResearchAndDevelopmentExpenseExcludingAcquiredInProcessCost.
One warning. Firms with no R&D mostly don’t report the tag at all, so in this data zero R&D shows up as a missing tag, not as a zero. Treat a missing tag as missing, not as zero, and say in DECISIONS.md that your median covers only firms that report R&D.
Stretch: your own question. Use the research question you brought. It has to be answerable, at least in part, from these three quarters of FSDS. Find the tags you need first and check their coverage in DATA_PROFILE.md before you build anything, because a tag that appears in 5 percent of 10-Ks will not support a figure. The stretch tier uses the same opening prompt structure, the same paper trail and the same verify checklist as the other two.

title: Lab 1: From FSDS to a Verified Figure
text:
Run it
Work in this order. Each step catches a different kind of mistake before it reaches the figure.

Start Claude in your data folder.
cd ~/stanford_lab && claude
Fill in the opening prompt. Open lab1_opening_prompt.md. It has six parts: DATA, JOIN, MEASURE, AGGREGATION, OUTPUT and PAPER TRAIL. Fill in the blanks for your tier in MEASURE and AGGREGATION, and change OUTPUT if you want a different figure. Leave the PAPER TRAIL part exactly as written, even if you’re short on time, because it is what produces DATA_PROFILE.md, DECISIONS.md and LOG.md. Paste the prompt and send it.
Read DATA_PROFILE.md as soon as it exists, before any measure is computed. Check the row counts, the uniqueness test (the number of rows should equal the number of distinct keys) and the tag coverage for each quarter. If anything looks wrong, stop and ask about it now. Press Esc if Claude is already moving on.
Look at the raw data. Ask for a plot of the firm-level ratio for each year, before any medians. Extreme values and impossible ratios (cash above total assets, say) are much easier to see here than in a median.
Make the figure. Let Claude draw it, then refine it in no more than three rounds.
Check one number against the 10-K. Pick one firm in your sample with a December year end. These are first-quarter files, so firms with other year ends (Apple’s ends in September) mostly appear only through their 10-Qs. Find its 10-K for one of your fiscal years on EDGAR, open the balance sheet (or the income statement, for R&D), and compare the value with the raw value in your data, before any division. Write the firm, the filing, the two numbers and whether they match into DECISIONS.md.
Work through the checklist below.







WarningCommon failure: a clean-looking figure



A figure with tidy axes and a sensible trend can still be wrong. A missing consolidated-row filter, for example, can inflate values and still produce a smooth line. Work through the checklist even when the figure looks fine.








TipVerify this: the Lab 1 checklist



The same list is in lab1_verify_checklist.md, with space to write in your checks. It is pass/fail and you grade yourself.

DATA_PROFILE.md written before the first figure: what one row is, a uniqueness test with both counts, tag coverage by quarter, and the rule for prior-year values and amendments
sub.txt and num.txt joined on adsh, with row counts before and after the join
Consolidated filter applied (segments and coreg blank, uom = USD), with row counts before and after, and no duplicate rows left
Only form = 10-K, and qtrs = 0 for stocks and qtrs = 4 for flows
Attrition table present, and every change in sample size explained in DECISIONS.md
Your tier’s tag decision in DECISIONS.md (Base: cash fallback and financial firms; Standard: missing R&D is missing, not zero; Stretch: coverage of your tags)
Raw firm-level values plotted before aggregating
Two sanity checks written down, each with a source: one benchmark comparison and one plausibility check
One number checked against the firm’s actual 10-K on EDGAR, and the result written down
Figure produced by a named script, and nothing exists only in the chat
A README that says how to rerun the pipeline from fsds/ to the figure, and at least one commit

The checklist

title: Before Class
text:
1. Install and sign in
You need four things on the laptop you will bring.

Claude Code on a Claude Pro or Max subscription, or with an Anthropic API key. A free Claude.ai account does not work with Claude Code. Install it with the native installer (macOS, Linux and WSL):
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Then run claude in any folder and follow the login steps. Homebrew (brew install --cask claude-code) also works. Anthropic’s setup guide has the current commands for every platform.
Python 3.9 or later with pandas and matplotlib. If you work mainly in Stata, install Python anyway. The labs use Python, and Claude writes the code.

Mac: python3 -m pip install --user pandas matplotlib. If pip refuses with “externally-managed-environment”, add --break-system-packages to the end.
Windows (inside Ubuntu/WSL): sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3-pandas python3-matplotlib unzip

git, which comes with macOS (run git --version; if it is missing, macOS offers to install it) and is already installed in Ubuntu/WSL. Tell git who you are, or your first commit in class fails with “Author identity unknown”. Run these once, with your own name and email:
git config --global user.name "Jane Doe"
git config --global user.email jdoe@stanford.edu
A GitHub account, free at github.com.

Windows users: Claude Code runs inside WSL2, a Linux system that Windows provides, not in PowerShell. Open PowerShell as administrator, run wsl --install, reboot, and then do everything on this page inside the Ubuntu window. Keep your project folders under your Linux home folder (cd ~), not under C:\Users.
The full course’s General Setup page walks through each step in more detail, with fixes for the common failures. It asks for the course access code, Barrios_AI2026. Ignore its WRDS steps for now.
How you know it’s done: in a terminal, each of these prints a version, ok or your email:
claude --version
python3 --version
python3 -c "import pandas, matplotlib; print('ok')"
git --version
git config --global user.email
and you can sign in to GitHub in a browser.

title: Before Class
text:
2. Run the smoke test
The smoke test checks that Claude Code can do real work on your machine: read and write files, run Python, and fetch a public SEC filing.

Download the starter pack and unzip it in your home folder, so the files end up in ~/stanford_starter/. Its README.md says what each file is for.

Mac: move stanford_starter.zip from Downloads to your home folder and double-click it, or run cd ~ && unzip ~/Downloads/stanford_starter.zip.
Windows (inside Ubuntu/WSL): cd ~ && unzip /mnt/c/Users/<your Windows user name>/Downloads/stanford_starter.zip

Make a new, empty folder and start Claude Code in it:
mkdir -p ~/setup_check && cd ~/setup_check && claude
Open ~/stanford_starter/setup_check_prompt.md. Copy only the text inside the prompt block, replace <TODO: Your Name your.email@stanford.edu> with your real name and email, then paste it into Claude Code and press Enter. Approve the permission prompts as they come up, reading each one before you say yes.

Claude writes a file called setup_check.txt. It records the versions of your tools, one number taken from a filing (Apple’s total assets in its 10-K for the fiscal year ended September 27, 2025) and the date.
How you know it’s done: setup_check.txt exists in ~/setup_check, it lists a version for each tool, and it gives Apple’s total assets with a link to the 10-K it came from. Open that link yourself, find total assets on the balance sheet, and confirm the number matches. We check every number the agent reports against the source, all session.
If the smoke test fails and you can’t fix it, email me at the address in the pre-class email no later than noon on Sunday, November 1. Include the error message and what you tried. A failed install is easy to fix by email two days ahead and very hard to fix in the room.

title: Before Class
text:
3. Download the data
Lab 1 uses three quarters of the SEC’s Financial Statement Data Sets (FSDS): 2016q1, 2020q1 and 2024q1. FSDS groups filings by the quarter the SEC received them, and most firms file their 10-K in February or March, so these files hold mostly fiscal years 2015, 2019 and 2023. Download them now so the room’s wifi can’t hold up the lab.



File
Size (zipped)




2016q1.zip
95.5 MB


2020q1.zip
96.6 MB


2024q1.zip
124.3 MB


Total
316.4 MB




Unzipped, the three quarters take about 1.6 GB, most of it in the three num.txt files. Leave at least 3 GB free.

The SEC refuses downloads that don’t say who is asking, and returns “403 Forbidden”. You identify yourself with a User-Agent of the form “Name email”. Make the folder you will use for Lab 1, make it a git repository that ignores the raw data, and download into it. Put your own name and email in the first line:
export SEC_UA="Jane Doe jdoe@stanford.edu"
mkdir -p ~/stanford_lab && cd ~/stanford_lab
git init
echo "fsds/" > .gitignore
bash ~/stanford_starter/download_fsds.sh
The .gitignore line keeps 1.6 GB of raw data out of git. The script downloads each quarter, unzips it into fsds/2016q1/, fsds/2020q1/ and fsds/2024q1/, and deletes the zip. It skips any quarter that is already there, so it is safe to rerun.
If you prefer to run the download by hand, this does the same thing:
export SEC_UA="Jane Doe jdoe@stanford.edu"
mkdir -p ~/stanford_lab/fsds && cd ~/stanford_lab
git init && echo "fsds/" > .gitignore
for q in 2016q1 2020q1 2024q1; do
  curl -fL -A "$SEC_UA" -o "fsds/$q.zip" \
    "https://www.sec.gov/files/dera/data/financial-statement-data-sets/$q.zip"
  unzip -oq "fsds/$q.zip" -d "fsds/$q" && rm "fsds/$q.zip"
  sleep 1
done
How you know it’s done: from ~/stanford_lab, ls fsds/*/ shows three folders, each holding sub.txt, num.txt, pre.txt, tag.txt and readme.htm, and ls -lh fsds/*/num.txt shows three files of roughly 390M to 470M each, and git status does not list fsds/.

title: The Session
text:
Block by block

Framing (20 minutes)
A chat window answers questions. An agent like Claude Code works in a folder on your machine: it reads your files, writes scripts, runs them, looks at the output and tries again. That makes it more useful for empirical work, and it means you need ways to control it. We cover four: a CLAUDE.md file that holds the project’s standing instructions, the permission prompts that ask before Claude edits a file or runs a command, plan mode (Shift+Tab) for agreeing on a plan before anything runs, and Esc to stop it mid-step. For the rest of the session, we check every number the agent reports against a source it did not produce.


Live demo 1 (25 minutes)
I take one research idea on FSDS data from an empty folder to a finished figure. Watch three things. The opening prompt has six parts (DATA, JOIN, MEASURE, AGGREGATION, OUTPUT, PAPER TRAIL), and you will reuse it in Lab 1. The paper trail gets written as the work happens: DATA_PROFILE.md before any figure, DECISIONS.md for every choice, and LOG.md for every step. And at least one thing goes wrong on purpose, such as a download refused with “403 Forbidden” for a missing User-Agent or duplicate rows that would double-count a firm, so you can see how the agent recovers and where I step in. The demo ends by checking one number against the actual 10-K on EDGAR.


Lab 1 (50 minutes)
You run the same loop yourself on the quarters you downloaded. Pick a tier (cash holdings, R&D intensity, or your own question), adapt lab1_opening_prompt.md, and finish with lab1_verify_checklist.md. Full instructions are on the Lab 1 page.


Demo 2 and Lab 2a (30 minutes)
A short demo applies the same steps to text: pulling the Risk Factors section (Item 1A) from a set of 10-Ks, counting a keyword, caching every download so a rerun fetches nothing twice, and writing a quality report that says which filings failed and why. Then you package your Lab 1 pipeline as a skill, .claude/skills/fsds-panel/SKILL.md, starting from SKILL_skeleton.md, and test that it fires in a fresh session on a request that doesn’t name it. Instructions are in Lab 2, Part A.


Lab 2b: verification drills (25 minutes)
Three short drills from lab2_verification_drills.md, all on your own project: the two-check credential audit, a clean-room referee that sees only your figure caption or paper-trail summary, and one deny rule in .claude/settings.json that you test. Instructions are in Lab 2, Part B.


Discussion and exit ticket (20 minutes)
We discuss three questions, one each on learning, on verification and on the market for papers, using the two readings and your own experience from the labs. The discussion questions for each paper are on the Readings page.
The exit ticket (exit_ticket.md in the starter pack) asks for four short answers:

one thing that broke today, and how you found out;
one thing you will verify next time before you trust a result;
one research task you will delegate to an agent;
one research task you won’t.
